entries.summary: Organization owners can now let people work on repository security advisories, including private vulnerability reports, through custom repository roles.
entries.text: Organization owners can now let people work on repository security advisories, including private vulnerability reports, through custom repository roles. You no longer have to make them repository administrators or give them the organization-wide security manager role. Four new permissions are available under Security when you create or edit a custom repository role: View security advisories: view draft security advisories, their status, and comments. Create, Edit, and Manage security advisories: everything in View, plus Create and Edit advisories, comment, manage collaborators, and create a temporary private fork. Accept private vulnerability reports and close or reopen security advisories: requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage. Publish security advisories and request CVEs: requires View or Create, Edit, and Manage. Assign the role to users and teams on only the repositories where they need it. The permissions apply to both repository security advisories and private vulnerability reports, so you can give a team access to the repositories they maintain without exposing advisories across your whole organization. A few things to know: Merging changes from a temporary private fork still requires a repository administrator or security manager. People with any of these new permissions can’t delete a temporary private fork. entries.summary: GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) 3.23 is now available and introduces new capabilities across the platform.
entries.text: GitHub Enterprise Server (GHES) 3.23 is now available and introduces new capabilities across the platform. Here are a few highlights in the 3.23 release: When working in GitHub Projects, you can create more precise project views by combining filters with logical OR, explicit AND, and parentheses for grouping. For example, (status:Done OR status:Todo) is:issue shows issues with either status. If your enterprise uses GitHub Secret Protection, you can detect unstructured secrets entirely within your network using AI secret detection on GHES, including in air-gapped environments. A self-contained, fine-tuned model runs on the appliance’s CPU without a GPU, hosted LLM, or outbound connection. This feature is in public preview and subject to change. As a developer, you can identify known malicious packages in PyPI, Maven, RubyGems, NuGet, Go, Rust, and Composer through the GitHub Advisory Database, in addition to npm. The database automatically ingests malware advisories from OpenSSF’s malicious-packages repository to expand coverage across these ecosystems. By default, Dependabot waits until a package version has been available on its registry for at least three days before opening a version update pull request. This cooldown gives maintainers and the community more time to detect and report compromised or buggy releases before users merge updates. entries.summary: Choose which repositories appear on the Dashboard with the new Favorite repositories section. If the new dashboard experience isn’t enabled, Top repositories remains unchanged.
entries.text: Choose which repositories appear on the Dashboard with the new Favorite repositories section. If the new dashboard experience isn’t enabled, Top repositories remains unchanged. Select Edit or Add repositories to open the picker. Search for repositories and select or deselect them. Your selections stay visible as you search. Select Save to apply your changes. New favorites are added to the end of your list. To discard your changes, select Cancel. Your favorites sync with your pinned repositories in GitHub Mobile. Changes you make in either place appear in the other after you refresh. You can pin up to 25 repositories across both experiences. If saving would put you over the limit, you’ll see an error and your list won’t change. Leave your feedback in the GitHub Community discussion. The post Pin your favorite repositories to your dashboard appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Pin your favorite repositories to your dashboard

entries.summary: GitHub Desktop now lets you sign in with more than one account on the same host, including GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Server, and GHE.com.
entries.text: GitHub Desktop now lets you sign in with more than one account on the same host, including GitHub.com, GitHub Enterprise Server, and GHE.com. This has been one of the most requested features in the Desktop community. With this release, you can: Add more than one account for a single host, with no fixed limit. Associate each repository with a specific account, so clone, publish, and Git operations use the right credentials automatically. Choose an account when adding or cloning a repository that multiple signed-in accounts can access, or let Desktop infer it when only one can. Change a repository’s account association at any time from repository settings or the repository list’s context menu. Existing repositories are migrated automatically to the account you were already using, so if you only have one account per host, nothing changes for you. To get started, download the latest (GitHub Desktop 3.7.0) and open Settings/Options > Accounts to add another account, then use the new account picker when cloning, publishing, or reviewing a repository’s settings. Learn more in GitHub Desktop’s authentication documentation. The post GitHub Desktop now supports multiple accounts per host appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: GitHub Desktop now supports multiple accounts per host

entries.summary: Your feedback has helped improve the new pull request Overview page since its November 5, 2026 public preview. Here’s what’s new!
entries.text: Your feedback has helped improve the new pull request Overview page since its November 5, 2026 public preview. Here’s what’s new! Clearer merge status and next steps Failed optional checks no longer make mergeable pull requests appear blocked. Previously missing merge requirements now show what needs attention. Readiness summary gives reviewers and visitors clearer guidance, including when no action is needed. Smoother review and comment interactions Checks and approvals now expand when clicked, instead of pinning a preview. Fixed overlapping previews and mobile interaction issues. Resolved review threads now collapse to keep completed conversations out of the way. Comments mentioning Copilot now better explain the action and selected model before submission. Activity details Force-push activity now links to the old and new commits so you can compare changes. Commit activity now includes timestamps so you can see when changes were made. Page layout and sidebar actions Source and target branches now stay visible on smaller screens. Edit links in the Development sidebar directly in Overview. Lock or unlock PR conversations directly in Overview. Fixed uneven spacing, misalignment, and sidebar gaps across screen sizes. Try the new overview page and give feedback To join, select the ✨ Try the Overview page button in the header. You can use the same menu to return to the classic overview during the preview. entries.title: Improvements on the pull request overview in public preview

entries.summary: Enterprise Live Migrations (ELM) from Azure DevOps Services to GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency is now generally available.
entries.text: Enterprise Live Migrations (ELM) from Azure DevOps Services to GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency is now generally available. You can move your repositories while your teams keep working, then cut over on your schedule. Manage migrations through the portal or CLI: Choose a guided experience in the Azure DevOps portal or script your migrations with the Azure DevOps CLI. Pre-migration validation and lifecycle tracking help you identify issues and monitor progress before cutover. Cut over on your schedule: ELM continuously syncs changes from Azure DevOps to GitHub, so developers can keep contributing throughout the migration. When you’re ready, complete the move with a brief cutover at a time that works for your teams. Bring your development history with you: ELM syncs Git history, branches, tags, and pull requests, including titles, descriptions, comments, and user history. Your Azure DevOps branch policies migrate as GitHub branch rulesets. Keep using Azure Boards and Azure Pipelines: You can have ELM create the Azure Boards connection and rewire Azure Pipelines to your migrated GitHub repository, reducing manual setup after cutover. Your work items and pipeline definitions stay in Azure DevOps. Ready to start your migration journey? Visit Microsoft’s ELM documentation to learn more and get started. The post Enterprise Live Migrations from Azure DevOps generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Enterprise Live Migrations from Azure DevOps generally available

entries.summary: Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 9 and RHEL 10 images for GitHub-hosted larger runners are now generally available.
entries.text: Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 9 and RHEL 10 images for GitHub-hosted larger runners are now generally available. Originally introduced in public preview in June 2026 in partnership with Red Hat, these images are now fully supported for production workflows in GitHub Actions. You can use RHEL images to run your workflows on the same operating system you deploy to, or as the foundation for custom images that include your required tools, dependencies, and configurations. To get started, create a new Linux x64 larger runner and choose your desired RHEL image under partner images. If you’ve been using RHEL images during the public preview, no action is required. Your existing runners and workflows will continue to work as-is. RHEL images are available for larger runners on GitHub Team and GitHub Enterprise Cloud plans. To learn more, see Managing larger runners and Using custom images. The post Red Hat Enterprise Linux runner images now generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Red Hat Enterprise Linux runner images now generally available

entries.summary: You can now stream enterprise audit logs to Amazon S3 using OpenID Connect (OIDC) on GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency (GHE.com).
entries.text: You can now stream enterprise audit logs to Amazon S3 using OpenID Connect (OIDC) on GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency (GHE.com). This extends the existing github.com capability, letting you authenticate without storing long-lived AWS credentials on GitHub. Learn how to set up audit log streaming to S3 with OIDC. entries.summary: GitHub CLI now supports GitHub Event Streams.
entries.text: GitHub CLI now supports GitHub Event Streams. With gh v2.105.0, you and your agents can wait for a pull request to change with a single command instead of polling it in a loop. Run gh event listen with a pull request URL and the events you care about, such as a submitted review. It creates the subscription, opens the stream and prints each event as a line of JSON. By default, it exits after the first event, so it slots into scripts and agent loops. Use --count to wait for several events, --follow to keep listening, and --timeout to stop waiting. Use --jq or --template to pull out just the fields you need. You can wait for submitted reviews, pull request state and head changes, merge conflicts and completed check suites. To manage subscriptions directly, use gh event subscription create, list, view, and delete. Agents discover the new commands on their own: gh pr create, gh pr view, gh run view, gh run watch, and gh api now suggest gh event listen instead of polling. Availability The gh event commands are in preview and may change. They require access to Event Streams, which is in preview on GitHub.com. To get access, sign up for the Event Streams waitlist. To get started, upgrade to gh v2.105.0 or later. For details, see the gh event manual and the Event Streams documentation, or run gh event --help. Share your feedback in the GitHub Community discussion. The post Wait for pull request events with GitHub CLI appeared first on The GitHub Blog.
entries.title: Wait for pull request events with GitHub CLI

entries.summary: You can now connect eight more services to Copilot using GitHub-verified MCP servers, or connectors, available in public preview.
entries.text: You can now connect eight more services to Copilot using GitHub-verified MCP servers, or connectors, available in public preview. They join more than 25 services you can already connect, like Slack, Figma, and Sentry. To see the full list, open Customize in the Copilot app or browse the Copilot customization page. New services you can connect Box: Search and manage content, and use Box AI. Buildkite: Work with pipelines and builds. Calendly: Manage scheduling and meetings. ClickUp: Track tasks and projects. Mixpanel: Explore product analytics. Supabase: Work with projects and databases. Webflow: Manage sites and content. Wix: Manage sites and business tools. For example, you can ask Copilot why your latest Buildkite build failed and have it fix the code in the same session, or have it check your Supabase schema before it writes a migration. Connect these services once, and you can use them across Copilot. Connect a service You connect these services the same way as any other connector: Copilot app: Open Customize and select Connect on the service you want. Copilot CLI: Run /mcp, switch to the Connectors tab, and select Connect on the service you want. VS Code: Open the Agents window, go to Customizations, and connect the service you want. github.com: Browse services on the Copilot customization page and select the service you want.
